slides.title: AST 101 Week 2: The Moon
body_text: Phases, eclipses and tides
Dr. Alex Morgan
slides.speaker_notes: Sky report: where is the Moon tonight, and when does it rise?

slides.title: Poll: Why Does the Moon Have Phases?
body_text: Earth's shadow
Clouds or dust
Changing distance
The angle between Sun, Earth and Moon
slides.speaker_notes: Most of the room votes for Earth's shadow every year. Keep the tally on the board.

slides.title: Half Lit, Always
body_text: The Sun lights one half of the Moon at all times
The phase is how much of the lit half faces Earth
That fraction depends on the Sun-Earth-Moon angle
slides.speaker_notes: Lamp-and-ball activity: a bare lamp is the Sun, a ball at arm's length is the Moon, your head is Earth. Turn slowly in a circle.

slides.title: Not Earth's Shadow
body_text: Earth's shadow points directly away from the Sun
A crescent Moon appears close to the Sun in the sky
The shadow reaches the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, at full moon
slides.speaker_notes: The crescent near the setting Sun is the observation the shadow idea cannot explain.

slides.title: The Phase Cycle
body_text: New, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous
Full, waning gibbous, third quarter, waning crescent
From new moon to new moon: about 29.5 days
One orbit relative to the stars: about 27.3 days
slides.speaker_notes: The two months differ because Earth moves along its orbit while the Moon goes around, so the Moon needs about two extra days to line up with the Sun again.

slides.title: Moonrise by Phase
body_text: New moon: rises at sunrise
First quarter: rises around noon, highest at sunset
Full moon: rises at sunset, sets at sunrise
Third quarter: rises around midnight, highest at sunrise
slides.speaker_notes: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day. Daytime Moons are normal.

slides.title: Eclipses
body_text: Solar eclipse: the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, at new moon
Lunar eclipse: the Moon passes through Earth's shadow, at full moon
Umbra: the dark central shadow; penumbra: the lighter outer shadow
slides.speaker_notes: Eye safety: never look at the Sun without a certified solar filter, eclipse or no eclipse.

slides.title: The 5 Degree Tilt
body_text: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit
The two orbits cross at two points called nodes
Eclipses happen only when a new or full moon falls near a node
That lines up about every six months: eclipse seasons
slides.speaker_notes: Two hula hoops tilted against each other show the nodes nicely.

slides.title: Annular and Total
body_text: The Moon's distance from Earth varies by about 10 percent
Near its farthest point it looks slightly smaller than the Sun: an annular eclipse
Near its closest point it can cover the Sun completely: a total eclipse
slides.speaker_notes: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away. That is why they look the same size.

slides.title: Tides
body_text: Two high tides about every 24 hours and 50 minutes
Caused by the difference in the Moon's pull across Earth
Near-side water is pulled toward the Moon more than Earth's center is
Far-side water is pulled less than the center, so it is left behind
slides.speaker_notes: Three runners on one rope, pulled from the front: the group stretches. That stretch is the two bulges.

slides.title: Spring and Neap Tides
body_text: Spring tides: new and full moon, Sun and Moon aligned, largest range
Neap tides: first and third quarter, smallest range
The Sun's tidal effect is a bit under half the Moon's
slides.speaker_notes: Spring has nothing to do with the season. Think of the water springing up.
